questions.question: Where are the factories that assemble Apple's products, and why is that a risk?
questions.answer:
Apple says that final assembly of substantially all of its hardware products is performed by outsourcing partners primarily located in Asia, and it also has manufacturing in whole or in part performed by outsourcing partners mainly in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam, as well as some partners and facilities in the U.S. [2][3]

This is a risk because Apple says it has reduced direct control over production and distribution, which can adversely affect the cost, quality, or quantity of products and its ability to respond to changing conditions. [2]

Apple also says disruptions to these partners or to manufacturing and logistics in those locations can reduce the supply of components or finished goods, and that failures, disasters, public health issues, geopolitical tensions, or other disruptions can interrupt supply and raise costs. [1][3][5]

questions.question: How does a weaker foreign currency against the dollar hurt Apple?
questions.answer:
A weaker foreign currency relative to the U.S. dollar hurts Apple because it reduces the U.S. dollar value of Apple’s foreign currency-denominated sales and earnings. [1][3]

It can also lead Apple to raise international prices, which may reduce demand for its products. [1][3]

If Apple chooses not to raise prices for competitive or other reasons, the U.S. dollar value of the gross margins on those sales would be adversely affected. [1][3]

The excerpts also say that foreign exchange movements can adversely affect gross margins and that hedging may not fully offset those effects. [1][3]

questions.question: What was the AI Diffusion rule and how would it have limited NVIDIA's exports?
questions.answer:
The AI Diffusion IFR was a U.S. government export rule published on January 15, 2025 that, unless modified, would have imposed a worldwide licensing requirement on NVIDIA products classified under certain ECCNs, including related software and technology, and on systems incorporating covered integrated circuits such as DGX, HGX, and MGX systems. [4][5]

It would also have divided the world into three tiers, with most countries becoming “Tier 2,” and would have created a complex licensing scheme for approvals. [2][4]

The rule would have limited NVIDIA’s exports by expressly restricting exports, reexports, and transfers of covered products to Tier 2 countries and to certain companies in Tier 1 that were headquartered in Tier 2 or had an ultimate parent headquartered in a Tier 2 country. [1]

It would have applied to products sold years ago, and it would have covered products such as A100, A800, H100, H200, H800, B100, B200, GB200, L4, L40S, and RTX 6000 Ada unless a license exception was available. [1][4][5]

The excerpts say these restrictions could reduce the market for U.S.-designed and manufactured computing products and services and negatively impact NVIDIA’s business, revenue, and financial results. [1][3]

claims.claim: The AI Diffusion IFR was a U.S. government export rule published on January 15, 2025.

questions.question: What risks does NVIDIA see in buying or investing in other companies?
questions.answer:
NVIDIA says buying or investing in other companies can divert capital and management attention, and there may be difficulty realizing a satisfactory return or the expected benefits, or no benefit at all. [1][5]

NVIDIA says acquisitions can lead to assumed liabilities, amortization expenses, impairment charges to goodwill, or write-downs of acquired assets, and can involve coordinating operations in countries where it does not currently operate. [1][5]

It says failure to obtain regulatory approval or to close an acquisition could cause stock price impact, fines, fees, or reputational harm. [1]

It also says acquisitions or investments could impair its ability to grow its business, develop new products, or sell its products, and its investments in publicly traded companies could create volatility in results and losses up to the value of the investment. [2][3]
